description: A plant hormone that functions as the central signaling agent in this review, regulating stomatal movements under water-deficit conditions and serving as the upstream trigger for ABA-mediated stomatal closure and related drought-response pathways.

The physiological process of closing stomata, which reduces gas exchange and water loss. In this text it is the primary ABA-responsive process and a key output of ABA signaling under drought and other environmental cues.
Dynamic opening and closing behavior of stomata. It is regulated by abscisic acid and other signaling inputs, especially under water-deficit conditions, and is central to plant water balance.
An environmental drought-like context in which ABA signaling regulates stomatal behavior. It provides the physiological setting that activates ABA-mediated responses.
Receptor molecules that detect abscisic acid and initiate downstream signaling. They are part of the ABA signaling core and are essential for transducing the hormone signal into stomatal responses.

The canonical family of abscisic acid receptors forming the sensing component of the ABA signaling core. They bind ABA and regulate downstream phosphatase and kinase signaling to control stomatal closure.
Protein phosphatases that act as core negative regulators in ABA signaling. They are inhibited upon ABA perception and are central to controlling SnRK2 activation and stomatal responses.
Protein kinases that function as core positive regulators in ABA signaling. Their activation downstream of ABA perception drives signaling events leading to stomatal closure.
The central molecular signaling module composed of PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors, PP2C phosphatases, and SnRK2 kinases. It mediates ABA signal transduction and is fundamental to stomatal regulation.
The downstream physiological response in which ABA signaling causes stomata to close. It is the main mechanistic outcome discussed in the review.
The intracellular signaling cascade initiated by ABA perception and propagated through receptor, phosphatase, and kinase components. It underlies stomatal regulation and broader ABA responses.

The baseline level of ABA signaling that contributes to stomatal regulation even in the absence of strong stress induction. It is discussed as important for responses to CO2 and vapor-pressure deficit.
The control of stomatal behavior by carbon dioxide levels, with basal ABA signaling implicated as a regulatory component in this process.
An atmospheric dryness condition hypothesized to influence stomatal regulation through basal ABA signaling. It represents an environmental context relevant to plant water loss control.
The broader network of signaling pathways that regulate stomatal behavior. The review discusses interactions between ABA and other pathways within this network.
A physiological endpoint reflecting the degree of gas exchange through stomata. The text notes that ABA signaling mechanisms can be used to manipulate this trait.
A plant performance endpoint describing the ability to withstand water limitation. ABA signaling manipulation is discussed as a strategy to enhance this outcome.
A physiological efficiency endpoint describing biomass or productivity gained per unit water used. It is presented as a trait that can be improved through ABA signaling-based manipulation.
An applied strategy using ABA signaling mechanisms to alter stomatal aperture behavior. It is relevant as an operational intervention aimed at improving drought-related plant traits.
A goal-directed intervention concept involving the use of ABA signaling mechanisms to improve plant drought resilience.
A goal-directed intervention concept involving ABA signaling-based manipulation to improve plant water-use efficiency.

Microscopic surface openings in plants that function as a regulated barrier in innate immunity. In this context, stomatal closure restricts bacterial invasion, while stomatal reopening can facilitate pathogenesis.
An immune-associated process in which stomata close to limit microbial entry into plant tissue. It is described as part of the plant innate immune response against bacterial invasion.
The host defense program in plants that detects microbial cues and activates protective responses such as stomatal closure. It serves to restrict bacterial invasion and infection.
The entry and spread of bacteria into host plant tissue, representing the infection-related endpoint that stomatal defenses aim to prevent.
Specialized plant cells in Arabidopsis that regulate stomatal aperture and participate in immune sensing of bacterial surface molecules.
The plant host model in which stomatal immune responses are studied. It provides the biological context for guard-cell signaling and bacterial defense.
Microbial-associated molecular patterns on bacteria that are perceived by plant guard cells to trigger immune signaling.
A plant receptor required for perception of bacterial surface molecules in guard cells, initiating downstream immune signaling leading to stomatal closure.
A signaling molecule required in the guard-cell immune response that contributes to stomatal closure after bacterial perception.
A guard-cell-specific kinase required for the immune signaling pathway that mediates stomatal closure in response to bacterial cues.
Bacterial pathogens of plants that attempt to overcome stomatal defenses and promote infection.
Bacterial factors evolved to counter plant stomatal immunity by inducing stomatal reopening and enhancing pathogenesis.
A process by which stomata reopen, counteracting closure and enabling bacterial entry as part of pathogen strategy.
The mechanism used by plant pathogenic bacteria to promote infection, including manipulation of stomatal aperture to facilitate entry.
The disease-relevant outcome resulting from microbial entry into host tissue, which stomatal defenses are described to prevent.

Specialized plant pores that regulate gas exchange, water vapour loss, photosynthesis, and pathogen entry; central to the paper’s discussion of closure and reopening dynamics under abiotic and biotic stress.
A protective process that reduces water loss in response to dehydration and limits pathogen entry, but when prolonged can impair photosynthesis and transpiration and alter apoplastic conditions.
The reversal of stomatal closure, dynamically regulated in changing environmental conditions; promoted by SCREW-NUT signaling to balance water loss and immune defense.

entity_name: SMALL PHYTOCYTOKINES REGULATING DEFENSE AND WATER LOSS (SCREWS)
description: Secreted peptide phytocytokines that act as immunomodulatory signals; sensed by NUT, recruit SERK co-receptors, and counter-regulate ABA- and MAMP-induced stomatal closure.
Cognate receptor kinase for SCREWs that mediates downstream signaling, recruits SERK co-receptors, and triggers phosphorylation events affecting stomatal closure control.
Phytohormone that induces stomatal closure in response to dehydration; its signaling is counter-regulated by SCREW-NUT signaling.
Microbial elicitor signal that induces stomatal closure as part of plant immune responses; antagonized by SCREW-NUT signaling.
Co-receptors recruited by SCREW-bound NUT to relay immune signaling in the stomatal regulatory pathway.
A phosphatase targeted by NUT-dependent phosphorylation; its activity toward OST1 is increased in the SCREW-NUT pathway.
A phosphatase targeted by NUT-dependent phosphorylation and functionally linked to regulation of OST1 activity in stomatal closure signaling.
Key kinase mediating ABA- and MAMP-induced stomatal closure; its activity is reduced by ABI phosphatases in the SCREW-NUT signaling context.
Ion channels whose activity is reduced downstream of SCREW-NUT signaling, contributing to stomatal reopening and altered guard-cell ion flux.
Abiotic stress condition that induces stomatal closure and triggers SCREW induction; relevant as an environmental driver of water-loss regulation.
Biotic stress condition that induces stomatal closure and SCREW signaling, linking immune defense with water-loss control.
Water loss through the apoplast promoted by SCREW-NUT signaling after dehydration or pathogen infection; functionally disrupts aqueous habitats for pathogens.
Downstream biological outcome limited by stomatal closure or by SCREW-NUT-mediated disruption of microorganism-rich aqueous habitats.
Carbon-fixation process reduced by prolonged stomatal closure due to restricted gas exchange.
Water-vapour loss process reduced by prolonged stomatal closure and modulated by stomatal reopening.
Physiological endpoint controlled by stomatal behavior; reduced by closure during dehydration but promoted by SCREW-NUT signaling to counter pathogen-friendly aqueous habitats.
Overall adaptive outcome optimized by the SCREW-NUT system through prevention of uncontrolled stomatal closure under abiotic and biotic stress.

The plant subject population used to test malate responses; these wild-type plants exhibited stomatal closure and increased S-type anion currents after malate treatment, serving as the reference biological model in the study.
A mutant plant population deficient in the SLAC1 anion channel gene; used to demonstrate that malate-induced stomatal closure and S-type anion current activation depend on SLAC1 function.
Isolated guard-cell-derived experimental preparation used to measure S-type anion currents and assess direct electrophysiological responses to malate.
A heterologous expression system used to test SLAC1 activity under extracellular versus intracellular malate application, enabling functional analysis of channel activation.
Application of malate outside the cell, described as the key stimulus that induces stomatal closure and activates SLAC1-mediated anion currents in guard cells.
Delivery of malate inside the cell, contrasted with extracellular application; it did not produce the same activation of S-type currents in the reported system.
The physiological endpoint measured in the study, representing reduced stomatal aperture in response to malate and dependent on SLAC1 and Ca2+ signaling.
The measurable opening state of stomata used as a functional readout of malate-induced closure.
Electrophysiological current output through slow anion channels in guard cells, increased by malate in wild-type plants and used as a functional indicator of SLAC1 activation.
The intracellular calcium level in guard cells, transiently increased by malate and implicated in signaling that supports SLAC1 activation and stomatal closure.
Calcium-dependent signaling process in guard cells that is stimulated by extracellular malate and contributes to sustained SLAC1 activation and stomatal closure.
SLOW ANION CHANNEL-ASSOCIATED 1, a guard-cell slow anion channel that is directly activated by extracellular malate and is essential for malate-induced stomatal closure.
The full gene/protein name corresponding to SLAC1, identified as the slow anion channel required for malate-induced stomatal closure.
The gene category describing SLAC1 as a slow anion channel gene involved in guard-cell anion transport and stomatal regulation.
A pharmacologic blocker used experimentally to inhibit calcium channel activity; it suppressed malate-induced stomatal closure, supporting a role for Ca2+ signaling.
A calcium-binding agent used to reduce available cytosolic calcium; it inhibited malate-induced stomatal closure, indicating dependence on Ca2+ signaling.

A plant hormone (ABA) investigated as the key regulatory agent in guard cell metabolism and water deficit acclimation. It is exogenously applied in the study and is functionally linked to glycolytic flux, sucrose cycling, and ABA-biosynthetic gene expression.

The specialized plant cell population analyzed as the experimental subject for metabolic, physiological, and transcriptional responses. Guard cells are the primary site where ABA-dependent metabolic regulation and water deficit memory were assessed.

The adaptive biological process by which plants adjust to recurring water deficit conditions. In this study, it is the central process influenced by ABA-mediated guard cell metabolism and altered by ABA deficiency.
The recurring drought-like stress condition used to challenge the plants. It serves as the environmental exposure scenario driving metabolic and transcriptional changes in guard cells.
The normal tomato genotype used as the reference plant population in the study. It was compared against the ABA-deficient mutant to evaluate ABA-dependent responses under water deficit.
Abbreviation for tomato wild type, representing the control genotype with intact ABA biosynthesis and normal acclimation responses.

An ABA-deficient tomato mutant used to test the role of ABA in guard cell metabolism and water deficit acclimation. It showed altered sugar and organic acid dynamics and weaker acclimation responses than wild type.

A physiological state characterized by reduced abscisic acid biosynthesis or availability. This state underlies the sitiens mutant phenotype and disrupts guard cell metabolic homeostasis and water deficit memory.
A class of primary metabolites measured in guard cells whose levels and accumulation/degradation dynamics were altered by ABA deficiency and water deficit.
Primary metabolic intermediates in guard cells whose abundance changed under water deficit and ABA deficiency, contributing to altered metabolic homeostasis.
The metabolic flow through glycolysis in guard cells, inferred from 13C-glucose labeling. ABA was required for glycolytic flux toward malate.
A key organic acid and metabolic endpoint of glycolytic flux in guard cells. Its formation from labeled glucose was used to infer ABA-dependent carbon partitioning.
A putative metabolic cycle involving sucrose turnover in guard cells. ABA acted as a negative regulator of this cycle according to the labeling experiment.
Genes involved in abscisic acid biosynthesis whose expression was higher in wild type guard cells after repeated water deficit cycles, indicating feedback regulation of ABA metabolism.
A physiological performance endpoint reflecting how efficiently leaves use water. It increased only in wild type after the second water deficit cycle, serving as an acclimation outcome.
A stress-memory process in guard cells and plants that influences responses to repeated water deficit episodes. ABA deficiency disrupted this memory and impaired acclimation.
The integrated metabolic state and pathways operating in guard cells, including sugar and organic acid homeostasis. It is regulated by ABA and altered by water deficit.
An isotope-tracing assay used to track carbon fluxes in isolated guard cells after ABA treatment. It provided evidence for ABA-dependent glycolytic routing and sucrose cycle regulation.
The experimental guard cell preparation used for metabolic tracing and ABA treatment. Isolation enabled direct measurement of guard cell-specific metabolic responses.
Externally supplied abscisic acid used to stimulate guard cell responses in the labeling experiment. It served as the experimental intervention to test ABA-dependent metabolic regulation.
A study assessment category describing physiological characterization of the genotypes under water deficit. It captures functional plant responses relevant to acclimation.
A study assessment category describing metabolic profiling of guard cells and plants. It was used to quantify changes in sugars, organic acids, and fluxes.
A study assessment category describing gene expression analysis in guard cells. It was used to evaluate ABA-biosynthetic gene expression under repeated water deficit.

A plant-specific SNF1-related protein kinase 2 family member that functions as a critical regulator in abscisic acid (ABA) signaling. It is described as a key molecular regulator of plant stress responses, growth control, and developmental processes, and is central to the review's discussion of ABA-activated kinase activity.

A plant-specific family of serine/threonine kinases involved in abiotic stress responses and ABA-mediated signaling. The family includes SnRK2 as a critical regulator and is functionally important for integrating stress signaling with plant growth and development.

A phytohormone that interacts with SnRK2 kinases to regulate plant organ development, stress responses, and growth inhibition under adverse conditions. It is a central signaling molecule in the abstract and is described as activating SnRK2 kinases.

The developmental process governing formation and growth of plant organs, described as being substantially controlled by the interaction between SnRK2 and ABA signaling. It is a key physiological outcome influenced by kinase-hormone crosstalk.

Non-living environmental stress conditions affecting plants, including drought-related stress, to which SnRK2 family members contribute a pivotal response. This process frames the stress-adaptation role of the kinase family.
A general plant stress response state discussed in the context of SnRK2 and ABA signaling. It encompasses environmental challenges that trigger signaling pathways affecting growth and physiology.

A specific abiotic stress condition mentioned as an example of stress in which SnRK2 and ABA signaling act synergistically. It is relevant as a major environmental trigger of plant adaptive responses.
A plant growth process specifically mentioned as being influenced by SnRK2 and ABA signaling during stress responses. It represents a developmental and physiological output of the signaling network.
A molecular signaling component whose control is described as being dual-regulated by SnRK2 kinases. It is part of the broader kinase signaling network affecting plant growth and development.

Overall growth of the plant, described as being promoted under optimal conditions and in the absence of ABA, but inhibited in response to ABA through SnRK2-mediated regulation. It is a central physiological endpoint in the review.
A favorable environmental context in which SnRK2 kinases promote plant growth. It serves as the contrasting condition to ABA-associated growth inhibition and stress response.
A hormonal context in which SnRK2 kinases are described as promoting plant growth. This condition is important for distinguishing the dual role of SnRK2 in growth regulation.
Activated SnRK2 kinases functioning downstream of abscisic acid signaling. This activated molecular state is emphasized as having emerging roles in plant growth and physiology.
The mechanistic physiological processes underlying the roles of ABA-activated SnRK2 kinases in plants. This term captures the functional basis of the signaling effects discussed in the review.
Plant guard cell protoplasts from Arabidopsis used as the experimental subject/population for phosphoproteomic and electrophysiological analyses of ABA signaling and stomatal closure.
The plant model organism in which MAP4K1 and MAP4K2 signaling was studied for regulation of stomatal closure under ABA and Ca2+-mediated conditions.
An abscisic acid treatment scenario applied to Arabidopsis guard cell protoplasts to trigger signaling events leading to stomatal closure.
A plant hormone used as the inducing agent for stomatal closure and ABA-responsive signaling in the study.
The environmental stress context under which ABA-induced stomatal closure limits water loss from plants.
The physiological process of closing stomata to reduce water loss; the central biological response investigated in relation to ABA, MAP4K1/MAP4K2, and Ca2+ signaling.
The plant physiological outcome reduced by ABA-induced stomatal closure under drought stress.
A proteomics-based phosphorylation profiling method used to identify ABA-responsive phosphorylation changes in guard cell protoplasts.
A phosphorylation signaling response induced by ABA, including phosphorylation changes in MAP4K1 that were assessed in the study.
A kinase whose ABA-responsive phosphorylation was down-regulated in SnRK2-disrupted mutants and whose Ser479 phosphorylation is required for promoting ABA-induced stomatal closure.
A kinase that, together with MAP4K1, positively regulates ABA-induced stomatal closure in Arabidopsis.
Mutant Arabidopsis lines with disrupted SnRK2 signaling used to assess dependence of MAP4K1 phosphorylation on SnRK2 activity.
A kinase signaling component required for ABA-responsive phosphorylation of MAP4K1 and upstream regulation of ABA signaling.
A specific phosphorylation site on MAP4K1 that is directly phosphorylated by SRK2E/OST1 and required for the stomatal closure phenotype.
A central ABA kinase that directly phosphorylates MAP4K1 at Ser479 and functions in ABA signaling.
Experimental assays used to demonstrate direct phosphorylation of MAP4K1 by SRK2E/OST1.
Genetic/functional analyses used to test the roles of MAP4K1 and MAP4K2 and the requirement of Ser479 for stomatal closure.
Externally applied calcium used to induce stomatal closure in map4k1map4k2 double mutants, revealing pathway specificity.
Hydrogen peroxide treatment tested as an alternative inducer of stomatal closure; it failed to induce closure in map4k1map4k2 double mutants.
Arabidopsis double-mutant plants lacking MAP4K1 and MAP4K2, used to determine the requirement of these kinases for stomatal closure responses.
Functional assays used to assess channel activity and determine the requirement of MAP4K1/2 for ABA-dependent activation of Ca2+-permeable channels.
Ion channels in guard cell protoplasts whose ABA-dependent activation requires MAP4K1/2 and contributes to Ca2+-mediated stomatal closure.
A calcium-dependent signaling pathway implicated in ABA-induced stomatal closure and regulated by the SnRK2/MAP4K signaling module.
A signaling module composed of SnRK2 and MAP4K kinases that regulates the Ca2+-mediated pathway in ABA-induced stomatal closure.

Plant epidermal cells that perceive environmental cues and transduce signals to regulate stomatal movement. They are the primary cellular subject in the abstract and the site where phosphorylation-dependent signaling controls ion channel activity and stomatal opening/closure.

The opening and closing of stomata, a regulated plant physiological process controlled by guard cell signaling. It is the central biological process discussed and is modulated by protein phosphorylation, ABA signaling, and blue light signaling.

A reversible post-translational signaling process in which phosphate groups are added to proteins. In this text it is described as an essential regulatory mechanism for guard cell signaling, stomatal closure, stomatal opening, and pathway cross-talk.

Membrane proteins in guard cells that control ion flux and thereby influence stomatal movement. The abstract notes early characterization of ion channels as key components of guard cell hormonal signaling and phosphorylation-dependent regulation.
Membrane transport proteins involved in guard cell hormonal signaling and ion movement. They are highlighted alongside ion channels as early targets of study in the regulation of stomatal movement.

Phosphorylation enzymes identified through genetic studies as important regulators of guard cell ion channel activities. Mutants defective in kinases indicate their functional role in phosphorylation-mediated stomatal signaling.

Dephosphorylation enzymes that counterbalance kinase activity and regulate phosphorylation states in guard cell signaling. Mutants of phosphatases are reported to be defective in controlling ion channel activities.
Proteins whose activity or function is controlled by phosphorylation in guard cells. They represent downstream molecular targets in the signaling network governing stomatal movement.
Abscisic acid-triggered closing of stomata, a stress-responsive plant process. The abstract states that protein phosphorylation plays an essential role in this process.
Blue light-triggered opening of stomata, a light-responsive plant physiological process. It is described as being essentially regulated by protein phosphorylation.

Hormone-mediated signaling in guard cells that regulates ion channel activity and stomatal behavior. It provides the broader signaling context for the phosphorylation-dependent mechanisms discussed in the abstract.
Interaction and integration among distinct signaling pathways controlling guard cell responses. The abstract highlights protein phosphorylation as the mediator of this pathway cross-talk.

An abiotic water-deficit stress scenario that serves as the central environmental condition in the review. It limits plant growth and productivity, triggers stomatal regulation, and drives hormone-mediated adaptive responses linked to drought tolerance and crop resilience.

The biological subject population discussed in the review. Plants respond to drought through adaptive signaling and physiological strategies, especially stomatal regulation and hormone crosstalk, to maintain water balance and photosynthetic efficiency.

A central physiological process controlling stomatal opening and closure. In this context it balances water conservation with photosynthetic efficiency and is governed by hormonal signaling during drought stress.
The process of closing stomata to reduce water loss. It is described as a drought-induced response principally regulated by abscisic acid and modulated by other phytohormones.

A physiological performance endpoint reflecting how effectively plants use water relative to carbon gain. The review states that hormonal crosstalk and stomatal dynamics ultimately determine this outcome under drought.
A resilience-related endpoint describing the ability of plants to withstand drought stress. It is presented as a downstream consequence of coordinated hormonal signaling and stomatal regulation.

An agronomic outcome referring to improved robustness of crops under drought conditions. The review frames hormonal regulation and stomatal control as mechanisms that can be harnessed to enhance this endpoint.
A class of plant signaling molecules that coordinate molecular, physiological, and biochemical responses during drought. They are central mediators of stomatal dynamics and adaptive stress responses.

The principal plant hormone regulator of drought-induced stomatal closure. It acts as a key signaling molecule in guard cells and is the main hormonal driver of stomatal responses under water deficit.
A phytohormone that modulates stomatal function during drought through synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other hormones, influencing guard cell signaling and drought responses.

Jasmonate-related signaling molecules that participate in hormonal crosstalk affecting stomatal behavior under drought stress. They can act synergistically or antagonistically with other phytohormones.
A plant hormone involved in modulating stomatal function during drought. It contributes to signaling crosstalk that shapes guard cell sensitivity and downstream adaptive responses.
A class of plant hormones that influence stomatal function and drought signaling networks. They are part of the hormonal interactions that regulate stomatal dynamics under stress.
Plant hormones that modulate stomatal behavior and interact with other phytohormones during drought. They contribute to the broader signaling network controlling stress adaptation.
Plant growth hormones that participate in the hormonal network influencing stomatal function during drought. Their interactions help shape adaptive signaling and physiological regulation.
The responsiveness of guard cells to abscisic acid signaling. This process is modified by hormonal crosstalk and is important for determining the magnitude of drought-induced stomatal closure.
The activity of membrane ion channels in guard cells that underlies stomatal movement. The review notes that hormonal signaling influences this process during drought stress.
Gene regulatory networks that integrate hormonal signals during drought. They are influenced by phytohormone crosstalk and contribute to stomatal regulation and adaptive responses.

The synergistic and antagonistic interactions among phytohormones that coordinate drought responses. It shapes guard cell sensitivity, ion channel activity, transcriptional regulation, and ultimately stomatal behavior.
Adaptive physiological and biochemical responses coordinated by hormones during drought. These responses are linked to stomatal dynamics and contribute to drought tolerance.
The broader regulatory process by which hormones control plant responses to drought. It is highlighted as a strategy to enhance drought resilience and crop improvement.

entity_name: HORMONAL REGULATION TO ENHANCE DROUGHT RESILIENCE
description: A proposed translational strategy that leverages hormonal control of stomatal and stress responses to improve plant performance under drought. It is framed as an emerging approach for crop improvement.
Leaf epidermal pores that regulate gas exchange with the atmosphere and serve as the physiological context for SLAC1-mediated signaling and closure.
The plant tissue setting in which stomata operate and where ABA-triggered stomatal signaling and closure occur.
External cues that elicit abscisic acid production/signaling in the leaf context, initiating the stomatal signaling cascade described in the abstract.
A plant signaling hormone induced by environmental stimuli that activates SLAC1 phosphorylation and downstream stomatal closure responses.
A plant anion channel central to stomatal signaling; its phosphorylation state regulates channel activity, guard-cell turgor, and stomatal opening/closure.
Phosphorylation-dependent activation process that increases SLAC1 channel function and links ABA signaling to stomatal closure.
The pressure within guard cells that is reduced by SLAC1 activity, contributing to stomatal closure.
Specialized leaf cells that determine stomatal aperture; their turgor pressure is modulated by SLAC1 activity.
The physiological endpoint resulting from ABA/SLAC1 signaling, characterized by reduced stomatal aperture.
Functional assay used to characterize AtSLAC1 channel activity and quantify phosphorylation-dependent enhancement.
The Arabidopsis SLAC1 channel variant analyzed functionally; used to identify phosphorylation sites and channel-activity enhancement.
Structural imaging method used to determine the BdSLAC1 structure at near-atomic resolution.
The Brachypodium SLAC1 channel variant analyzed structurally to reveal pore closure, basal-state conformation, and regulatory features.
Mapped phosphorylation sites identified in AtSLAC1 that are implicated in regulating channel activation.
The functional increase in SLAC1 activity observed when multiple phosphorylation sites are phosphorylated.
Conserved arginine residues in SLAC1 that are positioned for regulatory interaction with the N-terminal extension in the BdSLAC1 structure.
A regulatory region of SLAC1 that interacts with conserved arginines and contributes to channel regulation.
The closed pore conformation of BdSLAC1 observed in the basal structural state.
The resting conformational/functional state of BdSLAC1 prior to activation, characterized by closed pores and spring-loaded conformations.
Residues in BdSLAC1 that are in high-energy conformations and contribute to the spring-loaded basal state.
Energetically strained conformations of phenylalanyl residues that support the spring-loaded basal state of BdSLAC1.
The phosphorylation-dependent regulatory process that fine-tunes the equilibrium between basal and activated SLAC1 trimers.
Alternative oligomeric/conformational states of SLAC1 whose equilibrium is controlled by phosphorylation.
The degree of pore opening controlled by the equilibrium between basal and activated SLAC1 trimers.

A protein kinase (OST1) that functions as a key signaling regulator in ABA-induced stomatal closure. It activates downstream signaling components, including CPK15 and SLAC1, and is described as Ca2+-independent in this pathway.

An anion channel that is activated during ABA-induced stomatal closure. It is a downstream effector of OST1 and CPK15 signaling and its phosphorylation state controls anion currents and stomatal closure responses.

A Ca2+-dependent protein kinase that plays a central role in ABA-induced stomatal closure. It is activated by OST1 and Ca2+, phosphorylates SLAC1, and is essential for full stomatal closure and drought response.
An abscisic acid (ABA)-triggered biological process in which stomata close to regulate water loss and drought response. It is controlled by OST1, CPK15, and SLAC1 signaling.
A signaling mode describing OST1 activity that does not require calcium dependence. In this context, it contributes to activation of SLAC1 through CPK15-related signaling.
A kinase class that includes CPK15 and participates in activation of SLAC1 during ABA-induced stomatal closure. These kinases integrate calcium signaling into the stomatal closure pathway.
A threonine phosphorylation site on CPK15 that is phosphorylated by OST1. This residue is essential for ABA-induced stomatal closure.
The N-terminal region of SLAC1 containing multiple phosphorylation sites targeted by CPK15. Phosphorylation of this region activates SLAC1 anion currents.
Functional electrophysiological output of SLAC1 activation in oocytes. Increased anion currents indicate channel activation by phosphorylation.
A phosphomimetic form of SLAC1 that constitutively activates anion channel activity. It restores impaired ABA-induced stomatal closure in cpk15-1.
A phospho-dead form of SLAC1 that cannot mimic phosphorylation-dependent activation. It fails to restore impaired ABA-induced stomatal closure in cpk15-1.
The experimental cell system used to express SLAC1 variants and assess anion channel activity. They serve as the assay context for functional channel activation studies.
A physiological stress-response endpoint increased by mutation of CPK15. It reflects impaired stomatal closure and reduced drought tolerance.
A mutant Arabidopsis genotype lacking normal CPK15 function. It exhibits impaired ABA-induced stomatal closure and can be partially rescued by phosphomimetic SLAC1.
The plant model organism in which the ABA-induced stomatal closure pathway is studied. It provides the biological context for OST1, CPK15, and SLAC1 signaling.
Calcium ion signaling component that activates CPK15 and contributes to enhanced CPK15 activity toward SLAC1. It is part of the calcium-dependent branch of the pathway.

Specialized plant epidermal cells that integrate environmental signals and regulate stomatal opening and closing; they are the primary biological subject discussed in the review and the site where ABA and H2O2 signaling interactions occur.
The pore structures whose opening and closing are controlled by guard cells; stomatal closure is the key physiological endpoint linked to abscisic acid and hydrogen peroxide signaling.
External environmental input perceived by guard cells that triggers signaling responses leading to stomatal movement; it provides the contextual stimulus for the signaling pathways discussed.

A class of reactive oxygen-containing molecules that function as essential signal molecules in guard cells and mediate abscisic acid-induced stomatal closure; ROS are central to the signaling network reviewed.
A plant hormone that induces stomatal closure and interacts with hydrogen peroxide signaling in guard cells; it is a key upstream regulator in the signaling pathway described.
A reactive oxygen species that is generated and signals in guard cells, mediating ABA-induced stomatal closure and contributing to gene expression and signaling crosstalk.
The production of hydrogen peroxide in guard cells, discussed as part of the signaling cascade and as a prerequisite for downstream H2O2-dependent responses.
The signaling process mediated by hydrogen peroxide in guard cells, including its role in transmitting signals that influence stomatal closure and gene expression.
Changes in gene expression triggered by hydrogen peroxide signaling in guard cells; this process reflects downstream transcriptional responses to ROS signaling.
Interacting and overlapping signaling between ABA and H2O2 pathways in guard cells; it captures pathway integration and specificity in the response network.
The selective discrimination between ABA and H2O2 signaling responses in guard cells, highlighting how signaling outputs are distinguished within the pathway network.
The cellular process by which guard cells detect reactive oxygen species and convert that detection into signaling responses; it is a mechanistic focus of the review.
The plant population targeted by the broader biological significance of the signaling pathways, representing the intended agricultural application of improved ABA/ROS understanding.
A physiological performance endpoint in crop plants that may be improved through manipulation of guard-cell ABA and ROS signaling, especially under drought-related conditions.

Specialized plant epidermal cells that control stomatal pore opening and closure. In this context, they are the primary biological subject whose sensory systems integrate light, drought/ABA, and CO2 signals to regulate gas exchange, photosynthesis, and transpiration.

Dynamic pore structures regulated by guard cells to control gas exchange. Their opening and closure are central to plant physiological regulation and are the functional output of guard cell sensory signaling.
An environmental stimulus sensed by guard cells that influences stomatal behavior. It is part of the sensory context governing stomatal opening and closure.
A water-stress environmental condition that triggers guard cell signaling responses. In the text, drought is sensed indirectly via abscisic acid and contributes to stomatal closure.
A phytohormone that mediates drought signaling in guard cells. It functions as a signaling agent that stimulates stomatal closure and regulates downstream ion and water transport components.
An environmental gas signal sensed by guard cells. CO2 levels contribute to stomatal regulation and are part of the integrated sensory system controlling pore dynamics.
A core plant physiological process regulated indirectly by guard cell control of stomatal aperture. Stomatal opening affects CO2 uptake and thus photosynthetic efficiency.
The process of water loss through stomata that is regulated by guard cell-mediated pore opening and closure. It is a major physiological output of stomatal control.
A post-translational regulatory process highlighted as a mechanism used by guard cells to control ion channels and aquaporins during ABA-stimulated stomatal closure.
Membrane transport proteins in guard cells that are regulated during ABA-stimulated stomatal closure. They are key molecular effectors of ion flux and osmotic changes.
Water channel proteins involved in guard cell osmotic regulation. In the text, they are part of the molecular machinery regulated during ABA-stimulated stomatal closure.
The energy-dependent demands associated with stomatal opening in guard cells. These requirements are discussed as part of the physiological basis for aperture control.
The osmotic demands associated with stomatal opening in guard cells. They reflect the need for regulated solute and water movement to drive pore opening.

High-throughput molecular profiling approaches used to generate new information about guard cell physiology. In this context, omics contributes to integrated understanding of signaling and regulation.
Analytical and computational frameworks used to integrate guard cell data and infer physiological behavior. These approaches support system-level understanding of stomatal regulation.
The integrated functional biology of guard cells, including sensing, signaling, and stomatal regulation. It is the overarching process being advanced by omics and modeling approaches.

A major phytohormone in plants that functions as the central signaling ligand in the abstracted domain context. It regulates growth, development, and stress-responsive adaptive processes, and its perception initiates ABA signaling through receptor-mediated pathways.
A core developmental process in plants that is regulated by ABA signaling. In this context, ABA modulates growth as part of its broader role in developmental control and stress adaptation.
Plant developmental progression influenced by ABA. The text identifies ABA as a regulator of development, linking hormone signaling to coordinated physiological and morphological changes.
Stress-response programs in plants that are regulated by ABA. This includes responses to both non-living and living stressors, with ABA acting as a central mediator of adaptive signaling.

The environmental condition under which ABA synthesis and signaling are activated. It provides the context for ABA-mediated adaptive responses and post-translational regulation of signaling components.
The anatomical context in which ABA is synthesized under stress. The text indicates that ABA production occurs in various plant organs, supporting systemic signaling and adaptation.
A dormancy state in seeds promoted or regulated by ABA. It is one of the adaptive processes through which ABA influences plant survival and developmental timing.
A suppressive growth response associated with ABA signaling. It reflects ABA's role in reallocating resources and slowing growth during stress conditions.
A developmental aging process in leaves that is modulated by ABA. In the text, it is listed as an adaptive process influenced by ABA signaling.
A physiological process controlled by ABA signaling that reduces water loss and contributes to stress adaptation. It is a key downstream response of ABA perception.
The transcriptional output regulated by ABA signaling. ABA influences gene expression to coordinate adaptive responses under normal and stress conditions.
A core molecular component of ABA signaling that perceives ABA and initiates downstream signaling events. It functions upstream of PP2C and SnRK2 regulation.
A core negative regulatory component of ABA signaling. PP2C activity is controlled by ABA-dependent signaling and post-translational modifications that affect its activity and stability.
Core kinase components of ABA signaling that are activated or inactivated through phosphorylation/dephosphorylation. They are central effectors linking ABA perception to downstream responses.

The hormone signaling pathway initiated by ABA perception and mediated by receptor, PP2C, and SnRK2 core components. It integrates post-translational regulation to control plant stress and developmental responses.
The initial recognition step in ABA signaling in which ABA is detected by its receptor. This event triggers downstream activation/inactivation cascades.
A post-translational modification that regulates the activity of ABA signaling components. It is part of the activation/inactivation mechanism described for core signaling proteins.
A post-translational modification that counterbalances phosphorylation in ABA signaling. It contributes to the regulation of signaling component activity.
Post-translational modification and reversal processes that regulate the activity and stability of ABA signaling components. These modifications influence signaling output and protein turnover.
Functional state of ABA signaling components that is regulated by post-translational modification. Activity determines whether core proteins promote or suppress signaling.
Protein persistence or turnover of ABA signaling components, which is regulated by ubiquitination/deubiquitination and other post-translational modifications.
Baseline physiological context in which ABA signaling components and their post-translational regulation are discussed. It contrasts with stress conditions in the review.
Environmental context in which ABA signaling is especially active and its core components are regulated by post-translational modification.
